passage:
Subject: My ankle (please read before Saturday)

Dear Nilesh Sir,

I need to tell you something I've been hiding. At practice this week I said my ankle felt fine. It didn't. When I landed from the long jump on Thursday, I felt a sharp twinge and nearly cried, but I pretended I just tripped.
I wanted to be back so badly. I was scared that if I said it still hurt, you'd think I was weak or pick someone else for Saturday.
But my mother saw me limping and said if I make it worse, I could be out for much longer. That frightened me more.
So I'm telling you the truth. Can I sit out Saturday and go back to the doctor first?

Sorry,
Vandana

qa.q: When did Vandana feel a sharp twinge?
qa.a: Vandana felt it on Thursday when landing from the long jump.

qa.q: What made Vandana want to hide the pain at first?
qa.a: Vandana was scared the coach would think Vandana was weak or pick someone else, and badly wanted to be back.

qa.q: What was the wise choice Vandana made, and why?
qa.a: Telling Nilesh Sir the truth and asking to see the doctor first, because hiding pain could make the injury worse.

qa.q: How might Nilesh Sir feel reading this email?
qa.a: Nilesh Sir would likely be glad Vandana spoke up, and more worried about the ankle than about Saturday's team.

grounding: It shows a teenager eager to return who hid pain and risked a worse injury, then chose honesty over fear of being thought weak.

passage:
Sarita, you asked why I missed the whole season. Okay. So last June I hurt my wrist bowling in the nets. The doctor said to rest it. After a while I felt better, sort of, and the inter-school final was coming. I didn't tell anyone it still hurt. I strapped it myself and bowled eight overs.
By the sixth over I could barely grip the ball. I kept smiling so Coach wouldn't take me off.
Next morning my wrist was twice the size. Back to the doctor, and this time it was much longer out.
When I finally told Coach, she said, "Ritu, I'd never think less of you for being honest. I'd think less of a plan that breaks my best bowler."
I wish I'd said it before the final.

qa.q: How many overs did Ritu bowl in the final?
qa.a: Ritu bowled eight overs.

qa.q: Why did Ritu keep smiling during the sixth over?
qa.a: Ritu was afraid Coach would end the spell and wanted so badly to keep playing that Ritu hid the pain.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could fix it next time?
qa.a: Hiding the pain made the injury worse and kept Ritu out longer; telling Coach and following the doctor's pace next time would help.

qa.q: How did Coach feel about Ritu's honesty?
qa.a: Coach valued it and said she would never think less of Ritu for being honest, only of a plan that breaks her best bowler.

grounding: It shows a teenager who hid pain to play again, made the injury worse, and learned that the coach would not have thought less of the player for being honest.

passage:
Dear Ira Ma'am,
I need to tell you something I should have said last week.
At the district trials, I told you my ankle was fine. It wasn't. It still hurt from the sprain, and I strapped it tight and ran anyway, because I was scared you'd drop me from the squad if I missed another match. By the second half I was limping, and now the doctor says it's worse than before and I need three more weeks off.
I'm sorry I lied. I think I was so excited to play again that I stopped listening to my body.
If I'm honest from now on, will you still keep me in mind for the squad?
Suraj

qa.q: How many more weeks off does Suraj need now?
qa.a: Three more weeks.

qa.q: Why did Suraj hide the ankle pain?
qa.a: Suraj was scared of being dropped from the squad and too excited to play to listen to the pain.

qa.q: What does Suraj ask for, and why does it help?
qa.a: Suraj asks whether honesty will still count for the squad, opening a conversation that makes being honest easier next time.

qa.q: How might Ira Ma'am feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Ira Ma'am may feel disappointed that the injury got worse, but glad that Suraj told the truth.

grounding: Shows a teenager hiding pain to play again and making the injury worse, and learning that healing has its own pace and honesty with a coach matters.

passage: Kunal, you're the only one I'll tell this to properly, okay? It's me, Lavanya, and I did something really stupid last month. My wrist was still sore after the fall, but the state volleyball tournament was coming, and I'd been waiting all year. So I told Coach it was fine. I wrapped it in tape every morning and smiled through the pain. By the semi-final, I couldn't even hold a glass of water. The doctor said I'd made it much worse and now it's six weeks in a splint, not two. I cried in the car. What scares me most is that Coach will think I'm unreliable. But when I finally told her the truth, she said, 'I'd rather have you honest and healed than brave and broken.' I didn't expect that.

qa.q: How long is Lavanya's wrist in a splint now?
qa.a: Six weeks.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling while hiding the pain?
qa.a: Lavanya felt excited to play but also scared that Coach would think less of a player who pulled out.

qa.q: What does Coach's response teach about healing?
qa.a: That honesty about pain is valued, and healing at its own pace matters more than playing through injury.

qa.q: How might Kunal feel hearing this story?
qa.a: Kunal may feel worried and sympathetic, and glad to be trusted with it.

grounding: Shows a teenager hiding pain to keep playing and worsening an injury, and learning that a coach will not think less of honesty about healing.

passage:
Monday: Sabina, fifteen, felt a twinge in her hamstring at practice but said nothing. The inter-school final was in two weeks.
Wednesday: The pain was sharper. She ran anyway, gritting her teeth. Coach Sunaina noticed her limping in the cool-down and called her over. 'Is something hurting?' Sabina's eyes filled. 'If I say yes, I'll miss the final.' Sunaina sat on the bench beside her. 'I won't think less of you. Muscles heal at their own speed. If you push now, you'll miss the whole season.' She sent Sabina to the physio that afternoon.
Two Saturdays later: Sabina watched the final from the bench, cheering. Three weeks after that, she played the first league match, fully healed, and scored.

qa.q: When was the inter-school final?
qa.a: In two weeks.

qa.q: How did Sabina feel when Coach Sunaina asked if something was hurting?
qa.a: She felt upset and afraid, tearing up at the thought of missing the final.

qa.q: What did Coach Sunaina say that made honesty easier?
qa.a: That she would not think less of Sabina and that muscles heal at their own speed.

qa.q: How might Sunaina have felt watching Sabina score in the league match?
qa.a: She was probably proud and relieved that waiting paid off.

grounding: Shows a teenager tempted to hide pain to play, and a coach's reassurance that healing has its own pace making honesty easier.

passage: Irfan, sit down, you're limping and don't tell me you're not. Let your old uncle Joseph tell you about the summer I was sixteen. I sprained my ankle two weeks before the district football final. The coach said rest. But I could smell that trophy. So I wrapped it tight, told everyone it was fine, and ran on it every evening behind the church. On the day of the final I lasted twenty minutes. Then something went snap, and I spent that match, and the whole next season, on the bench. The worst part? When I finally told the coach, he just said, "Why didn't you tell me? I'd have planned around you." He wasn't angry. I'd been scared of nothing. So, Irfan. Tell me honestly. How is that knee?

qa.q: How long did Joseph last in the final?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: Why did young Joseph hide his ankle pain?
qa.a: He was eager and excited about the trophy, and scared the coach would think less of him or leave him out.

qa.q: What choice in the story could have changed Joseph's season?
qa.a: Telling the coach honestly about the sprain and resting, so the coach could plan around him instead of losing him for a season.

qa.q: How did Joseph's coach react when he finally heard the truth?
qa.a: The coach was not angry, more puzzled and disappointed, wishing Joseph had told him so he could plan around it.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager hiding pain to play again and making the injury worse, and learning the coach would not have thought less of him for honesty.
